name: Citation Graphs Over Time
title: Citation Graphs Over Time
answer: Citation graphs over time are maps of scholarly works where nodes are papers and directed edges are citations, with a time axis attached to each node and edge. They show how ideas spread, how fields cluster, and how the importance of a paper changes as later work cites it. The scope includes static snapshots and dynamic sequences, from a single paper's citation tree to whole-field networks. It also covers derived measures such as citation counts, co-citation, bibliographic coupling, and temporal bursts. A small library such as this site's 288 research papers can be drawn as one such graph, though most studies use much larger corpora.

sections.body: Citation graphs over time are maps of scholarly works where nodes are papers and directed edges are citations, with a time axis attached to each node and edge. They show how ideas spread, how fields cluster, and how the importance of a paper changes as later work cites it. The scope includes static snapshots and dynamic sequences, from a single paper's citation tree to whole-field networks. It also covers derived measures such as citation counts, co-citation, bibliographic coupling, and temporal bursts. A small library such as this site's 288 research papers can be drawn as one such graph, though most studies use much larger corpora.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: Citation graphs over time run on bibliographic databases and persistent identifiers. Sources include publisher metadata, DOI records, preprint servers, and open citation indexes. Storage needs graph databases or columnar tables that can hold nodes, edges, timestamps, and version history. Compute can range from a laptop for a few thousand papers to distributed systems for hundreds of millions of records. The site's own library is small enough for a single machine, but the same pipeline scales.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work starts with resolving each paper to a stable identifier and extracting its reference list. Then edges are created from citing paper to cited paper, with a timestamp from the publication date or the citation date if available. Analysts clean duplicates, merge author and venue names, and handle missing or ambiguous references. They then compute temporal metrics such as citation lag, burst detection, and network growth curves. Visual layouts often use force-directed or timeline-based views to show clusters and change over time.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Provenance matters because a citation graph is only as reliable as its source metadata. Rights issues arise from licensing of bibliographic records, full text, and any derived data that is redistributed. Risks include coverage bias, citation cartels, self-citation loops, and the mistaken treatment of citation counts as a direct measure of quality. A responsible practice records the data source, the extraction date, and the matching rules so that results can be audited. On this site, links go to the original paper rather than to a search tool, which keeps the chain of provenance visible.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Citation graphs over time are moving toward richer, more frequent updates and toward linking papers with datasets, models, and software. Temporal graph learning and dynamic network embeddings are being used to predict emerging topics and to trace the spread of methods. Open citation data and better identifier coverage are reducing gaps, though coverage remains uneven across languages and regions. The next step is likely to be interactive maps that let a reader move through time and see how a claim, method, or dataset travels. For a site that holds research papers, the same graph could connect papers to the artifacts they introduce.
